strengths: Novel core idea: casting value-stage attention aggregation as an unbiased Monte Carlo estimator (sampling rows of V from the post-softmax categorical distribution) rather than the common biased top-k truncation approach, with rigorous unbiasedness proofs, variance analysis (1/S scaling), and a vector-Bernstein concentration bound.

Solid variance-reduction contribution via stratified and systematic sampling (S²ANTA), with a proven variance-dominance theorem for the stratified variant and strong empirical validation that systematic sampling (which needs only one random number) performs comparably despite lacking the same guarantee.

Real, working CUDA kernels (S²ANTA-prop and S²ANTA-flash) that address the nontrivial GPU-parallelization challenge of sequential CDF-based sampling, with measured (not just theoretical) 1.5× decode-step kernel speedups over FlashInfer/FlashDecoding at 32k context on real hardware.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-7B, BitNet-2B), multiple benchmark families (GSM8K, MMLU, RULER long-context tasks), and multiple context lengths (4k/8k/32k), generally showing SANTA/S²ANTA recovers baseline accuracy at modest sample budgets while outperforming a top-k baseline, especially on tasks with diffuse attention (multi-hop QA).

Thoughtful complementary contribution (Bernoulli qKT with mean-group-query estimator for GQA) that extends sparsification to the score stage, plus a combined SANTA+Bernoulli-qKT experiment showing compounded savings.

Unusually thorough and transparent appendix material: detailed measurement/benchmarking protocol, prompting/grading procedures, ablations on per-layer sensitivity to sampling (one-hot attention diagnostic), and even a distributed RL experiment for learning per-layer sample budgets, all supporting reproducibility.

Honest treatment of limitations, e.g., explicitly showing SANTA loses its sparse-memory-access benefit in prefill (Appendix F/G), and candidly discussing the sample-waste tradeoff of the flash variant.
weaknesses: All GPU kernel latency benchmarks use batch size 1 only. Memory-bound decoding is most consequential in real serving settings with batching, where different sequences in a batch would sample different value-row indices, breaking the uniform/coalesced memory access patterns GPUs rely on; this practically important regime is not discussed or evaluated at all, undermining the generality of the 'memory-bound inference' framing in the title.

The 'multiplier-free'/energy-efficiency narrative is prominent throughout (title terminology, abstract, dedicated Section 3.5, pJ-based energy estimates) but is largely aspirational: current GPU kernels do not exploit the removal of multiplications (acknowledged by the authors), so the measured 1.5× speedup is driven entirely by memory-traffic reduction, and the energy argument rests on unverified back-of-envelope multiply/add cost estimates rather than measured hardware energy.

Only kernel-level (single decode-step) latency is reported; no end-to-end throughput or wall-clock generation-time results are given, despite the paper itself noting that realized gains are subject to Amdahl's Law -- leaving the practical, system-level benefit of the method unquantified.

The comparison against top-k is accuracy-only; no GPU latency/throughput benchmarks for top-k kernels are provided despite top-k requiring a nontrivial selection/sorting step, so the practical cost-accuracy tradeoff between SANTA and top-k in deployment remains unclear.

S²ANTA-flash requires 16× the sample budget of S²ANTA-prop (2048 vs 128) to match baseline accuracy at 32k context, indicating severe sample waste for the barrier-free variant; this substantially undercuts its practicality despite similar measured kernel speedup, and the paper does not explore ways to mitigate this waste.

Evaluation hardware is limited to a single GPU (RTX 6000 Ada) and context lengths up to 32k; no validation on other GPU architectures (e.g., data-center GPUs like H100/A100) or truly long contexts (100k+) that are increasingly relevant to long-context LLM deployment.

The Bernoulli qKT contribution is comparatively underdeveloped: no GPU kernel implementation or measured speedup is provided (only simulated feature-access percentages), and its strongest quantitative results rely on the heavily quantized BitNet 2B model, whose baseline SDPA accuracy on GSM8K (65.7%) is itself low, limiting the strength of the claimed benefit.

The manuscript relegates a very large amount of substantive content (proofs, additional experiments, kernel pseudocode, RL layer-budget study, prompting/grading protocol) to an unusually long appendix (23 pages), raising concerns about whether the 8-page main text is self-contained and whether the scope is appropriately focused for a single submission.

strengths: The core idea—treating post-softmax value aggregation as a categorical sampling problem to obtain an unbiased, gather-and-add estimator—is a reasonably original reframing of sparse attention, and the paper backs it with legitimate theory (unbiasedness, 1/S variance scaling, a vector-Bernstein concentration bound, and a variance-dominance result for stratified vs. i.i.d. sampling).

The empirical evaluation is unusually extensive for a systems paper: GSM8K, MMLU, and multiple RULER long-context tasks (FWE, NIAH, QA1, QA2) at 4k/8k/32k contexts, across three different models (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, BitNet 2B), with bootstrap confidence intervals reported throughout.

Real CUDA kernels were built (not just simulated), and decode-step latency is benchmarked against strong, widely used baselines (FlashInfer, FlashDecoding) with a clearly documented measurement protocol (Appendix Q), including a cache-thrashing procedure to avoid favorable cache-residency artifacts.

Useful diagnostic/ablation studies (one-hot attention layer sensitivity, RL-learned per-layer sample budgets, unique-key-count analysis) that give some mechanistic insight into which layers tolerate aggressive sparsification.
weaknesses: The measured benefit is narrow and modest: only a ~1.5x speedup on an isolated single-token decode-step attention kernel at batch size 1 on one GPU (RTX 6000 Ada); there is no end-to-end model-serving throughput/latency number (e.g., tokens/sec in vLLM/TensorRT-LLM with realistic batch sizes), so the paper never demonstrates the headline memory-bound inference benefit it is framed around. The paper itself notes end-to-end gains are 'subject to Amdahl's Law' but never quantifies this, leaving the central practical claim unverified.

The 'multiplier-free'/energy-efficiency narrative that frames the abstract and title is almost entirely aspirational: the actual GPU kernels do not realize multiplier-free execution or energy savings (acknowledged in Sec 3.4/3.5), and the pJ-based energy estimates (Appendix H) are back-of-envelope arithmetic, not measured. This creates a gap between the paper's framing and its demonstrated contribution.

Scope creep and dilution: the paper bundles SANTA, S2ANTA-strat/sys, S2ANTA-prop/flash kernels, Bernoulli qKT, mean-group-query estimation, and a Kubernetes-based RL layer-budget search into a single paper. Several of these (Bernoulli qKT in particular) have no actual GPU kernel or measured speedup—only theoretical operation counts—undermining the 'kernel-level' story told for SANTA. The RL schedule-search (costing ~1000 GPU-hours) is a tangential curiosity that is not integrated into the main method or evaluation.

Accuracy-matching operating points (S=128 for prop, S=2048 for flash) are selected post hoc as 'smallest S that matches baseline' on the exact same tasks used for evaluation, which risks a form of test-set tuning; there's no held-out validation protocol for choosing S, and no sensitivity analysis showing how brittle this choice is to task/domain shift.

Robustness to adversarial or peaked attention distributions is not analyzed: sampling-based approaches are inherently vulnerable to missing rare-but-critical tokens (e.g., true single-needle retrieval with very peaked attention), and the chosen RULER tasks/metrics (e.g., partial-credit FWE, substring-match QA) may mask such failures; NIAH in particular shows only marginal/no improvement over baseline, suggesting the method's strength is task-dependent in ways not fully characterized.

The Bernoulli qKT component reports ~30-60% L2 relative score error yet claims near-baseline downstream accuracy only on BitNet 2B/GSM8K and a narrow long-context slice (4k context only, unlike SANTA's 32k evaluation); this is a much weaker and narrower validation than for SANTA, undermining confidence that the technique generalizes.

Important baselines for contextualizing the contribution are only partially explored: quantized KV-cache methods, which the paper claims are 'orthogonal' and stackable, are never actually combined and tested together with SANTA, so the orthogonality claim is unverified empirically.

The writing/structure buries essential methodological details (e.g., full derivations, kernel pseudocode, prompting/grading protocols) in ~15 dense appendices, which, combined with the breadth of disparate contributions, makes the paper feel like several under-matured ideas stapled together rather than one well-developed contribution.

strengths: Solid theoretical grounding: the paper proves unbiasedness of SANTA and its stratified/systematic variants, derives a 1/S variance scaling result, a vector-Bernstein concentration bound, and a formal variance-dominance theorem for stratified sampling over i.i.d. sampling — unusually rigorous for a systems-oriented paper.

Genuine systems contribution: the paper identifies and solves a real parallelization challenge (sampling from a global CDF breaks the associative split-KV pattern used by FlashDecoding-style kernels) via two concrete kernel designs (proportional allocation vs. speculative/deferred-normalization), and demonstrates measured 1.5x decode-step kernel speedups against strong, realistic baselines (FlashInfer, FlashDecoding) rather than only simulated FLOP savings.

Extensive multi-axis empirical validation: accuracy is checked across multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, BitNet 2B), multiple tasks (GSM8K, MMLU, RULER FWE/NIAH/QA1/QA2) at multiple context lengths (4k/8k/32k), with bootstrap confidence intervals, and compared to a biased top-k baseline — showing SANTA's unbiasedness is advantageous particularly for multi-hop QA where information is not concentrated in top-k keys.

Thorough reproducibility and transparency: detailed kernel-benchmarking protocol (hardware, driver/software versions, cache-thrashing protocol to avoid favorable cache effects, tensor shapes), exact prompts/parsing/grading procedures, dataset/model licenses, and extensive pseudocode for the kernels are all provided in the appendix.

Thoughtful supplementary analyses that strengthen the empirical story: layer-wise sensitivity ablations (one-hot attention probing which layers tolerate approximation), an RL-based adaptive per-layer sample-budget scheme that independently rediscovers the same sensitive layers, and measurement of unique keys sampled (showing caching potential beyond the nominal S budget).
weaknesses: The headline motivation (memory-bandwidth-bound decoding due to streaming the full KV cache) is only partially addressed: SANTA still requires computing exact attention scores over all nk keys (reading the full K matrix) to form the categorical distribution before sampling V, so only the V-side of KV bandwidth is reduced. This caps the achievable end-to-end speedup well below what the abstract's framing might suggest, and the paper's own kernel numbers (≈1.5x, not closer to the theoretical multi-x reduction implied by >90% V-access reduction) reflect this bottleneck without the paper fully foregrounding it in the main narrative.

Bernoulli qKT, the mechanism meant to address the complementary key/score-stage bottleneck, is not validated with an actual GPU kernel or latency measurement; it remains a PyTorch-level/theoretical demonstration (Section 5), explicitly noted as "forward-looking." This leaves the paper's claim of sparsifying "both branches" of attention systems-unvalidated, and the combined SANTA+Bernoulli experiment (Table 7) is only accuracy-based with no measured speedup.

All kernel latency experiments use batch size 1 on a single GPU (RTX 6000 Ada); no batched-decoding results are reported, which is the dominant real-world LLM serving regime. Gather-based sparse access patterns may interact poorly with batching/memory coalescing, and it is unclear whether the reported speedups persist (or even hold directionally) under realistic batched inference.

The reported "accuracy-matching" operating points (e.g., S=128 for prop, S=2048 for flash, B=8 for Bernoulli qKT) are selected post hoc per benchmark suite to match SDPA within confidence intervals; this is a reasonable way to report results, but it is unclear how a practitioner would choose S a priori for a new task/domain without such oracle access, limiting operational guidance.

The Bernoulli qKT estimator exhibits large raw approximation error (~30% L2 error even for stratified sampling at B=4) yet downstream accuracy is preserved only in a heavily quantized model (BitNet 2B) and, to a lesser degree, Llama 8B; it is unclear how robust this tolerance is across architectures, and no theoretical variance-reduction guarantee is given for the stratified Bernoulli estimator (only an empirical plot).

Only kernel-level (single decode step) latency is reported; no end-to-end, multi-step generation throughput or wall-clock comparison is given, so the realized benefit in an actual serving pipeline (accounting for Amdahl's law effects the authors themselves note) remains unquantified.

strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically important problem (memory-bandwidth bottleneck in long-context autoregressive decoding) with a conceptually clean solution: unbiased stochastic sampling of the post-softmax distribution to sparsify value-cache reads and eliminate value-stage multiplications.

Strong theoretical grounding: unbiasedness proofs, variance scaling analysis (1/S), a vector-Bernstein concentration bound, and a formal variance-dominance theorem for stratified sampling versus i.i.d. sampling.

Goes beyond a purely algorithmic proposal to deliver actual GPU CUDA kernels (S2ANTA-prop and S2ANTA-flash) that address a genuine systems challenge (parallelizing sequential sampling/CDF computation on GPU), with measured (not just theoretical) decode-step kernel speedups (~1.5x) and end-to-end batched decode-latency speedups (~1.25x) that are further explained via a simple, checkable Amdahl-style bandwidth model.

Extensive empirical validation across multiple axes: GSM8K, MMLU, RULER (multiple 8k/32k tasks), LongBench v2, and HumanEval; multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, BitNet 2B); comparisons against top-k baselines showing SANTA's advantage in long-context multi-hop settings.

Honest and thorough limitations analysis, including explicit acknowledgment that SANTA does not yield sparse memory benefits in prefill (backed by a unique-row-coverage experiment), detailed tile-sensitivity and same-state fidelity analyses (Appendix U) explaining when S2ANTA-flash underperforms, and clear statements that hardware/batching/context length affect realized gains.

Rich set of supplementary analyses (layer-wise one-hot ablation, REINFORCE-learned per-layer sample budgets, unique-key-count analysis, empirical variance validation) that add scientific depth beyond the core speedup claims and suggest promising directions (adaptive per-layer/per-tile budgets).
weaknesses: The core idea of stochastically sampling attention weights to approximate AV is conceptually related to prior Monte Carlo attention approximations (e.g., Kim & Ko, 2022, cited by the authors); the paper's novelty is concentrated in GPU-friendly variance-reduction (stratified/systematic sampling) and kernel engineering rather than a fundamentally new estimator.

Reported speedups (1.5x kernel-level, 1.25x end-to-end) are relatively modest for the added complexity (custom kernels, budget tuning, sample-waste tradeoffs between prop/flash variants), and are demonstrated on only one GPU (RTX 6000 Ada, batch size 6); no empirical validation on datacenter GPUs (A100/H100) where bandwidth/compute ratios differ, despite claims of general applicability.

The GQA worst-case analysis reveals that unique value-row access can reach 12.5%-97.9% (for Bernoulli qKT with GQA) rather than the much sparser per-head numbers headlined in the abstract/intro, somewhat tempering the 'extreme sparsity' framing.

Although the paper claims complementarity with KV-cache compression/selection/retention methods (ShadowKV, Quest, DuoAttention, MLA), no empirical combination or integration experiments are provided; this is left entirely to future work, weakening the practical significance claim.

Bernoulli qKT (score-stage sparsification) is a secondary, underdeveloped contribution: no GPU kernel or measured speedup is provided for it, and its combination with SANTA (Table 9) shows a nontrivial accuracy drop (63.8% vs 65.7% baseline) at practical value-budget settings, undermining its practical readiness relative to the more mature value-stage method.

Systematic sampling (S2ANTA-sys), which is the variant actually used in the headline kernel results, lacks a theoretical variance-reduction guarantee (only empirical support in Appendix D), leaving a gap between the paper's strongest theory and its strongest empirical results.

Energy-efficiency claims rely on back-of-envelope calculations using generic per-operation energy numbers (Horowitz, 2014) rather than direct hardware energy measurements, making the 'multiplier-free, energy-efficient inference' framing more aspirational than validated.

The need to select an accuracy-matching sample budget per kernel/task (S=128 vs S=2048 for prop vs flash) adds deployment complexity, and the one-hot ablation study demonstrating strong layer-wise sensitivity suggests uniform per-layer budgets (as used in main experiments) are suboptimal, though the RL-based adaptive schedule is only explored as a proof-of-concept on one model/dataset.

strengths: The core idea—replacing exact post-softmax value aggregation with an unbiased stochastic sampling estimator (SANTA) and its variance-reduced variants (stratified/systematic)—is theoretically clean and well-grounded; unbiasedness and 1/S variance scaling are proven rigorously (Appendix A), with a Bernstein-type concentration bound provided.

The paper engineers two distinct GPU kernel strategies (S2ANTA-prop and S2ANTA-flash) to address the genuine systems challenge of parallelizing sequential CDF-based sampling on GPUs, and reports measured (not merely simulated) kernel speedups (~1.5x) and end-to-end batched decode speedups (~1.25x) on real hardware.

Breadth of empirical validation is substantial: GSM8K, MMLU, HumanEval, RULER (8k/32k), and LongBench v2, across two model families (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B, BitNet 2B), with bootstrap confidence intervals reported throughout.
Useful diagnostic ablations (one-hot layer sensitivity, learned per-layer sample-budget via RL) provide some mechanistic insight into which attention layers tolerate approximation.

Extensive appendices on fidelity analysis (tile-size/tile-support sensitivity) and unique-key coverage give honest discussion of when S2ANTA-flash underperforms, rather than only presenting favorable numbers.
weaknesses: The headline accuracy-matching operating points require surprisingly large sample budgets (S=128 for prop, S=2048 for flash at 32k context), and accuracy collapses sharply at small S (e.g., GSM8K near-zero accuracy at S=2-8 in Table 4); this undercuts the 'extreme sparsity' narrative and raises the question of how much the realized speedup is actually attributable to sparsity versus to replacing multiplies with adds within a still fairly dense working set, especially for S2ANTA-flash whose required budget is 16x that of S2ANTA-prop.

The 'multiplier-free'/energy-efficiency framing is a central selling point of the paper (appears in title/abstract/Section 3.6) but is never actually measured on hardware; the energy argument rests entirely on a back-of-envelope calculation using 2014-era process-node pJ estimates (Horowitz, 2014) applied to a 2025 GPU, which is a weak basis for the claimed 5x energy reduction over top-k.

Despite extensive related-work discussion of competing KV-selection/retention systems (ShadowKV, OmniKV, DuoAttention, QUEST, H2O, SparQ, MagicPIG), the empirical comparison is limited to naive top-k attention; none of these more sophisticated and widely used baselines are benchmarked for accuracy or latency, making it hard to judge SANTA's practical standing relative to the actual state of the art in long-context KV efficiency.

The reported end-to-end speedup (1.23-1.25x) is considerably more modest than the kernel-level speedup (1.5x), and is only demonstrated at a single batch size (6) and a single GPU (RTX 6000 Ada); scaling behavior under production-style continuous batching, paged attention, or datacenter GPUs (A100/H100) is only speculated about via an Amdahl-style model, not measured.

Section 5 (Bernoulli qKT) is presented as a 'contribution' in the abstract/intro but is not implemented as a kernel and shows large approximation error (30-70% relative L2 error in Appendix C.1) and inconsistent behavior across models (BitNet needs near-full key access while Llama needs much less), which is left unexplained; this component feels underdeveloped relative to its prominence in the framing.

Accuracy 'matches baseline' claims on LongBench v2 and some RULER subtasks rest on bootstrap CIs that are wide (e.g., ±1-3.4%) and based on only 3 runs over a few hundred prompts, so the claimed parity is statistically weak and could mask real degradation, particularly for S2ANTA-flash at lower budgets.

The paper exhibits significant scope creep (distributed Kubernetes RL infrastructure for layer-wise budget search, extensive appendices) that is tangential to the core contribution and dilutes focus without materially strengthening the central claims about decode-time speedup.

The prefill-is-dense, decode-is-sparse experimental design (used for the main kernel/latency results) is reasonable for decode-bound workloads but is not clearly reconciled with Section 4's accuracy experiments where SANTA is applied to both prefill and decode, creating some inconsistency in what is actually being validated as 'the method'.

strengths: Strong theoretical foundation: the paper provides rigorous unbiasedness proofs, variance-reduction theorems for stratified sampling, and dimension-free concentration bounds (Appendices A, B), grounding the empirical claims in formal guarantees rather than heuristics.

Genuine systems contribution: unlike many 'theoretical speedup' papers, the authors implement real CUDA kernels (S²ANTA-prop and S²ANTA-flash) and report measured decode-step latency against strong, widely-used baselines (FlashInfer, FlashDecoding), showing consistent ~1.5x kernel speedup and 1.25x end-to-end batched decode speedup that is further explained by a simple, verifiable Amdahl-style bandwidth model.

Extensive and diverse empirical validation across GSM8K, MMLU, RULER (multiple sub-tasks at 8k/32k), LongBench v2, and HumanEval, with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals throughout, multiple models (Llama-3.1-8B, DeepSeek-7B, BitNet 2B), and fair comparisons against a deterministic top-k baseline that reveal task-dependent trade-offs (e.g., SANTA variants outperforming top-k on multi-hop QA).

Thoughtful and honest ablations that go beyond the core claims: layer-wise sensitivity analysis via one-hot attention, a REINFORCE-based layer budget allocation experiment, unique-key-count analysis, and tile-size/tile-support sensitivity studies for the flash kernel variant, which transparently reveal when and why the speculative kernel underperforms (sample waste).

High reproducibility effort: detailed appendices specify exact prompts, answer-extraction/grading protocols, hardware/software versions, dataset licenses, and kernel pseudocode, which substantially aids independent verification.
weaknesses: All kernel and end-to-end latency results are measured on a single GPU (RTX 6000 Ada); no validation on datacenter-class hardware (A100/H100) is provided, despite the paper explicitly motivating the work around large-scale, bandwidth-bound serving where such GPUs are most relevant. The claim that benefits 'remain relevant' on such hardware is speculative.

SANTA/S²ANTA only sparsifies the value-aggregation stage; the score stage (qKᵀ) still requires reading and computing over the full K matrix (and even the prop kernel's Pass 1 computes exact scores over all nk keys), so the realized bandwidth savings are confined to roughly half of the attention pathway. This fundamental limitation is acknowledged but somewhat underemphasized relative to the headline sparsity percentages reported.

The Bernoulli qKT score-stage method, while conceptually appealing, is explicitly described as a 'forward-looking' idea not integrated into the actual speedup-producing kernels; no systems-level (kernel/latency) validation of the combined SANTA+Bernoulli approach is given, and the limited accuracy results for the combination (Table 9) show non-trivial degradation at low budgets, leaving the practical value of the combination unclear.

S²ANTA-flash, one of the two proposed kernel designs, requires a substantially larger sample budget (S=2048 vs. S=128 for prop) to match baseline accuracy due to 'sample waste,' and the tile-sensitivity analyses in Appendix U show its fidelity is highly dependent on how concentrated attention mass is—raising questions about its robustness and practical preference over the proportional-allocation variant in deployment.

No direct empirical comparison is made against other prominent KV-cache reduction/retention methods mentioned in related work (H2O, Quest, DuoAttention, ShadowKV); the relationship is discussed only qualitatively as 'complementary,' leaving the practical combined benefit (e.g., stacking SANTA with a cache-eviction method) unverified.

End-to-end batched decoding evaluation uses a modest batch size (6) and a single workload configuration; broader batch-size/throughput scaling curves would better support the claim that benefits grow with batch size and context length.

Energy savings claims (Section 3.6, Appendix H) rely on rough back-of-envelope pJ-per-op estimates from a 2014 hardware reference rather than measured energy on real accelerators, weakening the practical significance of the 'energy-efficient inference' framing in the abstract.
